takeaway: BQSim fuses repeated quantum gates with decision diagrams, converts them to GPU-friendly sparse matrices, and schedules many input-state simulations through one reusable CUDA task graph.
background: A classical quantum-circuit simulator computes ideal state amplitudes without running quantum hardware. Testing and verification often apply one fixed circuit to hundreds or thousands of different initial states.
villain: Most simulators optimize one state at a time, while CPU-oriented decision diagrams and separately launched simulations fail to exploit GPU parallelism across a batch of input states.
approach: BQSim uses decision diagrams to fuse gates according to the multiply-accumulate cost of batched simulation. It then chooses CPU or GPU conversion per fused gate and emits ELL sparse matrices, whose regular rows suit a batched GPU sparse-matrix kernel. A CUDA task graph reuses the optimized circuit and multiple GPU buffers to overlap kernel execution with transfers across successive batches.
impact: The authors claim that optimizing once at the circuit level and reusing a GPU execution graph makes full-state simulation more practical for applications that explore many inputs to the same circuit.

evaluation.overview: The authors measure end-to-end runtime, preprocessing stages, batch-size scaling, power, and ablations for ideal full-state simulation of circuits from MQT-Bench.
evaluation.implemented: A classical CPU/GPU software prototype with decision-diagram gate fusion, hybrid CPU/GPU DD-to-ELL conversion, CUDA batched sparse-matrix kernels, and Taskflow over CUDA Graph.
evaluation.setting: Experiments use one 48 GB RTX A6000 GPU, a 16-core Intel i7-11700 host, and 128 GB RAM. Sixteen circuits spanning 6–21 qubits are each simulated with 200 batches of 256 randomly generated state vectors; Qiskit Aer and FlatDD, which lack batch simulation, run eight processes for input-level parallelism.

results.text: Across the sixteen circuits with 200 batches of 256 inputs on one RTX A6000, the authors report that BQSim was 3.25× faster in geometric mean than cuQuantum’s gate-level batched API.

In the four-circuit, ten-batch ablation, the authors report that converting decision diagrams to ELL accelerated BQSim by 5.55×–35.08× compared with traversing GPU-resident decision diagrams directly.

limitations: The study covers ideal full-state simulation of many inputs to one fixed circuit, reaches at most 21 qubits on one A6000, and does not evaluate noisy-circuit or multi-GPU execution. Gate fusion and format conversion are one-time costs amortized over many batches, while the hybrid conversion threshold is hardware- and circuit-dependent.
phd_group_signal: The work reflects a GPU-systems methodology that co-designs representation, kernels, and scheduling, then isolates each layer with conversion tests, scalability experiments, power measurements, and ablations.

claims.text: BQSim performs batch-cost-aware decision-diagram gate fusion, converts fused gates to ELL using a per-gate CPU/GPU choice, executes ELL sparse-matrix multiplication over batches of state vectors, and schedules reusable kernels and transfers as a CUDA task graph.

The design assumes fused gate matrices have sufficiently uniform nonzeros per row for ELL, and its preprocessing pays off when one optimized ideal circuit is reused across many batches whose state vectors fit the available GPU memory.
